533.title: Stop being whirled around
533.hook: don't let outside things distract you; make time to learn something good (Meditations 2.7)
533.howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often set a single aim for the day and cut one habitual distraction, using the time to study something worthwhile.

segments.voice: Yesterday: throw away the thirst for books, not the books. Your line was enough reading. What did you put down, and what did you live by instead? Day five hundred thirty-three.

Eleven browser tabs. A half-written email. A notification, then another. You check the news, then the weather, then the news again, in case it changed in the last four minutes. A day like that can leave a person worn out by evening, with nothing finished to show for it. Book two has a word for that state, and it's a physical one: whirled around. Spun, like a top, or a leaf in a gust of wind. Today: stop being whirled around.
screen: `ELEVEN TABS, NO PROGRESS.` → `A LEAF IN A GUST.` → `STOP BEING WHIRLED AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Section seven opens by asking: do the things outside you distract you? Marcus was running an empire at war. If anyone had a reason to be distracted, it was him. Second, the cure. In Long's translation: "Give thyself time to learn something new and good, and cease to be whirled around." Notice the cure isn't, empty your mind. It's, give yourself something good to learn. A mind with nothing to hold onto spins. A mind with something worth learning has a center. Third, the second mistake. Then Marcus catches himself, because there's a trap on the other side. Some people, he says, wear themselves out with activity, and yet have no aim to which they direct every movement and every thought. They're busy, but they're still spinning. Being whirled around by outside things is one mistake. Whirling yourself around with aimless busyness is the other. Both look like motion. Neither goes anywhere. Fourth, the aim. What Marcus wants is a center: one aim that every movement points toward. Here he doesn't say what his own aim was. It doesn't have to be grand. A good day, a kind word, a piece of work done well. The spinning slows when there's something in the middle. So today's practice is small. Not to stop all motion, just to stop one spinning thing. One tab, one loop of checking, one busy task that doesn't actually point anywhere. And in the time you get back, learn one good thing.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the day's spinning come to mind: the checking, the switching, the half-done things. Don't fight them. Just watch them circle, like leaves in wind. Now find the center: one aim for today, simple and real. Let your breath settle around it. Then pick one spinning thing you'll stop when the bell rings, and one good thing you'll learn instead. The bell holds the time.
Stop being whirled around. Marcus's cure for distraction: learn something new and good, and give every movement an aim, so busyness isn't just more spinning. Today's word.
Your line: stop spinning. Close one tab, one loop, one aimless task today, and use the time to learn one good thing. Day five hundred thirty-three.

534.title: Attend to your own soul
534.hook: no one is unhappy for ignoring another's mind, only their own (Meditations 2.8)
534.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism do brief check-ins during the day, noticing their own impressions and reactions instead of trying to decode what others are thinking.

segments.voice: Yesterday: stop being whirled around, by outside things or by aimless busyness. Your line was stop spinning. What did you stop, and what did you learn instead? Day five hundred thirty-four.

A colleague says fine in the meeting, and nothing else. Not fine, let's do it. Just fine, and a look at the table. What did that mean? Is he annoyed? Was it something said last week? A question like that can follow a person home and sit with them at dinner. A lot of a day can go into trying to read other people's minds. In book two, Marcus makes a blunt observation about where that attention would be better spent. Today: attend to your own soul.
screen: `FINE. AND A LOOK AT THE TABLE.` → `READING OTHER PEOPLE'S MINDS.` → `ATTEND TO YOUR OWN SOUL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Section eight is two sentences. Hardly anyone, Marcus says, has been seen to be unhappy because they didn't notice what was going on in someone else's mind. But people who don't follow the movements of their own minds are bound to be unhappy. Second, the honest word. He doesn't say never. He says hardly anyone, or seldom. Of course there are times when misreading someone costs us. Marcus isn't pretending otherwise. He's pointing at which kind of attention pays. Third, the movements of the mind. For the Stoics, the mind is always moving. An impression arrives: he's annoyed with me. Then comes a moment when you agree to it, or don't. Then an impulse: send a worried text, go cold, rehearse an argument. Watching those movements, catching the impression before you agree to it, is the heart of the practice. Epictetus said it in his handbook, which opened this year: test the impression first. Marcus is writing the same lesson to himself. Fourth, where to point the flashlight. You can't see into his mind, however long you replay the word fine. You can see into your own. You can notice the story you're telling, the fear under it, the reaction you're about to have. That's the one mind you can actually tend. This isn't selfishness. Elsewhere in this same book, Marcus says we were made to work together, like hands or feet. Attending to your own soul is what makes you safe to be around. It's how one word in a meeting stops running your afternoon.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Check in with yourself, the way Marcus suggests. What's moving in your mind right now? A worry, a plan, a replay of a conversation? Name it, quietly. Then ask: is this about my own mind, or am I guessing at someone else's? If you're guessing, gently bring the flashlight back. What are you feeling, under the guess? Stay there. Attend to your own soul. Few are made unhappy by not reading another's mind; those who don't watch their own are bound to be. Today's word.

535.title: Ready to leave
535.hook: act, speak and think as one who could leave life at any moment (Meditations 2.11)
535.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism use the thought of death as a prompt not to postpone what matters, such as apologies, thanks and time with people they love.

segments.voice: Yesterday: attend to your own soul, the flashlight turned inward. Your line was mind my own mind. What did you find moving in there? Day five hundred thirty-five.

Some people who travel for work keep a bag half packed. Toothbrush, charger, a clean shirt. When the call comes, they can be out the door in ten minutes, without panic. Nothing important is left undone, because they keep it that way. In book two, Marcus writes himself a note about living like that. Not about wanting to go. About being the kind of person who could, without leaving a mess of unsaid things behind. Today: ready to leave.
screen: `A BAG HALF PACKED.` → `NOTHING IMPORTANT LEFT UNDONE.` → `READY TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Section eleven begins: since you could leave life at any moment, let that shape every action, every word and every thought. It's not a threat. It's an editing rule. If this might be the last thing I do, is this how I want to do it? Second, the reasoning. Marcus then thinks out loud about what leaving means. If there are gods, he says, departing isn't something to fear, because they wouldn't bring you into harm. If there were no gods, or they didn't care, why would he want to live in a world empty of them? Then he says plainly what he believes: they do exist, and they do care. People today read that passage from many places: some share his faith, some don't, some aren't sure. What all of them can notice is that he reasoned his way to calm, not away from the question. Third, what isn't the point. Life and death, praise and blame, pain and pleasure, money and its lack, he says, happen to good and bad people alike. So they can't be what makes a life good or bad. What makes it good is how you live it. Fourth, ready. Ready doesn't mean waiting to go, or wanting to. It means not leaving the important things for later. The apology. The thank you. The I love you you assume they know. A traveler with a half-packed bag isn't hoping to leave. They're just free to live without dread. That's the life the entry points toward: not a shorter one, a fuller one, lived so that any moment could be the last one and still be all right.

segments.voice: This can feel heavy, so go gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you'd regret leaving unsaid or undone if today were your last ordinary day. A thank you. An apology. Editing rule. Marcus's name for living as if you could leave life at any moment: let that shape every act, word and thought, and leave nothing important for later. Today's word.
Your line: ready. Do one thing today you'd hate to leave undone: say the thank you, make the call, mend the small break. Day five hundred thirty-five.

536.title: How fast things vanish
536.hook: how quickly all things disappear, bodies and memories alike (Meditations 2.12)
536.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism reflect regularly on impermanence, letting it loosen the grip of status and pleasure and sharpen their attention to the present.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the editing rule, the bag half packed. Your line was ready. What did you do that you'd hate to leave undone? Day five hundred thirty-six.

A corner store becomes a phone shop. A teacher retires and moves away. The song everyone hummed one summer stops being played. Far enough back in an old photo album, there are faces nobody in the family can name. It happens so gradually that it only shows when someone looks back. In section twelve, Marcus looks back, and looks hard, and starts with a sentence that's almost a sigh. Today: how fast things vanish.
screen: `THE CORNER STORE IS GONE.` → `FACES NOBODY CAN NAME.` → `HOW FAST THINGS VANISH.`

segments.voice: First, two kinds of vanishing. How quickly everything disappears, Marcus says: bodies, out of the world, and then the memory of them, out of time. First the person goes. Then, more slowly, the remembering goes. Second, what dazzles. Then he looks at the things that pull at us hardest: things that tempt with pleasure, things that frighten with pain, things people brag about. How cheap they are, he says, how perishable, how quickly gone. It's the same trick we've seen on this path with the emperor's purple robe, looking at something until its glamour wears off. Third, death itself. And what is dying? If you look at it alone, he says, stripping away all the imaginings we pile onto it, you'll see it's simply a work of nature. And to be terrified of a work of nature is, in his words, to be like a child. He doesn't mean grief is childish. He means the dread we add on top of the plain fact. Fourth, what's near. The entry ends by pointing at something to look into, not an answer: how a human being comes near to God, by what part of himself, and when. He doesn't name the part here; a few days ago we met the one he calls the ruling part. Readers on other paths will name it differently, or not at all. But the turn is worth noticing. After everything that vanishes, he points at what's closest. Not to escape the vanishing. To stand in it, steadily, and say: so quickly. And then, still, to live today.
screen: `BODIES GO; THEN MEMORIES GO.` · `WHAT DAZZLES IS PERISHABLE.` · `DEATH: A WORK OF NATURE.` · `HOW DO WE COME NEAR TO GOD?` · then, large: `SO QUICKLY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that's already gone. A place, a voice, a habit, a version of yourself from ten years ago. Let yourself see it clearly for a moment. Notice how quickly it went, and how it still lives a little in you. Don't hurry past the feeling. Then come back to this breath, here, which is also going, and is still here. The bell holds the time.
How fast things vanish. Marcus: bodies leave the world, and then their memory leaves time, so quickly. Death, seen plainly, is a work of nature. Today's word.
Your line: so quickly. Once today, look at something ordinary, a mug, a face, the light, and say inside: so quickly. Then enjoy it. Day five hundred thirty-six.

537.title: No prying
537.hook: nothing is more wretched than going round prying into others' souls (Meditations 2.13)
537.howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often cut back on gossip and checking up on others, and turn that attention to their own character instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: how fast things vanish, bodies and then their memory. Your line was so quickly. What ordinary thing did you look at and enjoy? Day five hundred thirty-seven.

It's eleven at night, and you're four years deep into the vacation photos of someone you don't even like. Or you're piecing together, from a coworker's tone and a calendar invite, exactly what's going on between those two. Nobody asked you to. It's not useful. It doesn't even feel good. And yet it's oddly hard to stop. Marcus knew the pull. A few days ago he said to watch your own mind. Today he goes further, and he doesn't soften it. No prying.
screen: `FOUR YEARS INTO SOMEONE'S PHOTOS.` → `NOBODY ASKED YOU TO.` → `NO PRYING.`

segments.voice: First, the strong word. Nothing is more wretched, Marcus says, than a person who goes round and round everything, digging into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and trying to guess what's in the minds of the people around them. Wretched is a big word. He means it. The prying mind is busy, restless and never full. Second, the poet. The phrase about the things beneath the earth comes from the Greek poet Pindar. Plato once borrowed it to describe a philosopher whose mind ranges over everything. Marcus turns it around: that endless searching, pointed at other people's business, is a misery, not a virtue. Third, what's enough. Instead, he says, it's enough to attend to the guiding spirit within you, and to serve it sincerely. Keep it clean of turmoil, of carelessness, and of resentment toward gods and people. You have one inner life to look after. That's a full-time job. Fourth, how to see others. And when you do look at other people, Marcus says, look with affection, because they're your kin. Sometimes, even, with a kind of pity, when they don't know good from bad, which he calls a blindness no smaller than not telling black from white. Notice the order. Not suspicion, not curiosity, not judgment. Affection first. Pity, when it's called for. Prying has no place in that list. Not my business isn't coldness. It's a way of giving people the privacy you'd want, and giving yourself back the evening.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one place your curiosity tends to go where it isn't needed. A profile you check. A rumor you follow. A relationship you keep analyzing. Picture the pull of it. Now picture closing that door, gently, and turning back toward your own inner room. What needs tending in there today? Then think of the person you were prying into, and send them one plain thought of goodwill instead. The bell holds the time.
No prying. Marcus says nothing is more wretched than digging into other people's minds; tend your own inner spirit, and see others with affection. Today's word.
Your line: not my business. Skip one bit of prying today: one profile, one rumor, one question that isn't yours to ask. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

538.title: The soul's self-harm
538.hook: the soul harms itself most when it turns against others in anger (Meditations 2.16)
538.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism treat anger and resentment as harms to their own character first, and work to loosen grudges for that reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no prying, and affection instead. Your line was not my business. What did you leave alone? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

There's an old saying, often repeated and of uncertain origin, that holding a grudge is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to get sick. Marcus never heard it, but his notebook circles the same idea. In section sixteen he lists the ways a soul wounds itself, and one of them is anger. A word first: Marcus means this as a picture of what anger and falseness do inside us. If the phrase self-harm touches something painful in your own life, please reach out to someone you trust today. Now, the entry. The soul's self-harm.
screen: `DRINKING THE POISON YOURSELF.` → `A LIST OF INNER WOUNDS.` → `THE SOUL'S SELF-HARM.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. The soul does violence to itself, Marcus says, and he names five ways. The striking thing is the direction. We usually think of harm as something done to us. Marcus is interested in the harm we do from the inside. Second, a growth on the world. The first way is when the soul becomes, in his image, like a swelling or a tumor on the universe: when it rages against whatever happens, as if it could pull away from the whole of nature it belongs to. Third, turning against others. The second way is today's center: when the soul turns away from another person, or moves against them meaning to hurt them, the way angry people do. Marcus's point is that anger at someone else wounds the one who carries it. We were made, he said earlier in this book, to work together, like two hands. A hand that strikes the other hand hurts the body it belongs to. Fourth, masks and aimlessness. The other ways: when the soul is overpowered by pleasure or pain; when it plays a part, saying or doing anything false; and when it acts with no aim at all, carelessly, without thinking. Notice that all five are harms done from inside. And notice how practical that is. If the harm comes from inside, so can the repair. A grudge softened by one degree is one less wound. Don't harm myself is a surprisingly kind way to say: let it go a little.
screen: `FIVE WAYS THE SOUL HURTS ITSELF.` · `RAGING LIKE A GROWTH ON THE WORLD.` · `TURNING AGAINST OTHERS IN ANGER.` · `PLEASURE, MASKS, AND NO AIM.` · then, large: `DON'T HARM MYSELF.`

Now, without excusing anything they did, breathe into that place and let it soften by one degree. Just one. You're not doing this for them. You're putting down a little of what you've been carrying. Your line: don't harm myself. When a grudge flares today, remember who it's really hurting, and soften it, even slightly. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

539.title: A stranger's sojourn
539.hook: life is a war and a traveler's stay; what can guide us? philosophy (Meditations 2.17)
539.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus treat life as a stay in borrowed rooms, and keep a guide, philosophical or religious, that they return to each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tumor, the grudge that hurts the one who holds it. Your line was don't harm myself. Did a grudge soften, even by a degree? Day five hundred thirty-nine, the end of a week.

This week, book two kept pressing. Stop spinning. Mind your own mind. Live ready to leave. See how fast things vanish. Don't pry. Don't wound yourself with anger. Now comes the last entry of the book, and it gathers everything into one long breath. Life is short, Marcus says, and slippery, and strange. He piles up image after image, and then, at the bottom of the pile, he asks a single question: then what can guide a person through it? Today: a stranger's sojourn.
screen: `A WEEK OF BOOK TWO.` → `ONE LONG BREATH.` → `A STRANGER'S SOJOURN.`

segments.voice: First, the pile. Section seventeen begins: the time of a human life is a point. Its substance is always flowing. The senses are dim. The body is decaying. The soul is a whirl, fortune is hard to read, and fame is without judgment. Everything of the body is a river, and everything of the soul a dream and smoke. Second, the line in today's title. In Long's translation: "life is a warfare and a stranger's sojourn, and after-fame is oblivion." A war, because it's struggle. A stranger's sojourn, because we're travelers here, staying a while in a place that isn't ours to keep. Third, the question. "What then is that which is able to conduct a man? One thing and only one, philosophy." For Marcus, philosophy wasn't a subject. It was a way of living: keeping the spirit within unharmed, above pleasure and pain, doing nothing without aim, nothing false, not depending on what others do or don't do, accepting what comes, and meeting death calmly, as nature's work. Fourth, your guide. Listeners on this path will answer the question differently. Some are guided by a faith, some by a teacher, a text, a practice, a person. Marcus named his. The question is the gift: if life is a traveler's stay, what are you traveling by? That's where book two ends: a long list of what slips away, and one thing to hold on to.
screen: `A POINT, A RIVER, A DREAM.` · `A WAR, AND A STRANGER'S STAY.` · `WHAT CAN GUIDE? PHILOSOPHY.` · `WHAT DO YOU TRAVEL BY?` · then, large: `A TRAVELER'S STAY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture yourself as a traveler, staying a while in a borrowed room. The room is your life: your body, your days, your people. Nothing in it is yours to keep, and all of it is yours to care for. Now ask: what guides me here? A faith, a teacher, a book, a practice, a person, a few hard-won rules. Name it, quietly. If you're not sure, that's honest too; sit with the question. The bell holds the time.
A stranger's sojourn. Marcus calls life a war and a traveler's stay, and asks what can guide us. For him, one thing: philosophy. Today's word.
Your line: a traveler's stay. Treat one thing today as borrowed, a room, an hour, a person's attention, and take good care of it. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is short and hard.
what it means: life is a borrowed stay, a struggle and a journey, and the real question is what you travel by.
what a scholar hears: 2.17 piles up images of flux, then defines philosophy as keeping the daimon, the spirit within, unharmed.
